opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on whether you're talking about inference or training, because those are really different stories right now.

On inference, I think Huawei's Ascend chips are genuinely usable. If you're a Chinese lab and you've got a model that's already trained, serving it on Ascend hardware is workable. The raw compute on something like the 910-series parts isn't embarrassing; it's maybe a generation or so behind Nvidia's best on paper. And inference is a more forgiving workload. You can quantize, you can batch cleverly, you can throw more chips at the problem. The pain is mostly software: getting your serving stack, your kernels, and your attention implementations tuned for CANN instead of CUDA. But that's an engineering cost you pay once and then amortize, and there's a lot of pressure in China to pay it.

Training is where it gets much harder. Frontier pretraining isn't just about the FLOPs of one chip. It's about running tens of thousands of them in lockstep for months without things falling over. That stresses interconnect, memory bandwidth, and reliability, and above all the maturity of the software stack. Nvidia's real moat is the fifteen-plus years of CUDA, NCCL, and all the debugging tools and institutional knowledge that let a team find out why its loss spiked at step 400,000. When people talk to labs that have tried large training runs on Ascend, the recurring theme is reliability and tooling. It's not that the chips can't do the math. It's that everything around them is less mature, so your effective utilization is lower and your engineers spend a lot more time fighting infrastructure.

There's also the supply question, which I think is underrated. Even if the chips were perfect, Huawei is constrained on advanced manufacturing and especially on high-bandwidth memory. So the question isn't just "is a single Ascend chip good?" It's "can you get enough of them, at good yields, to build a frontier-scale cluster?" That's where export controls actually bite.

So my overall take is that they're practically useful today. They're a real option for inference and for a lot of post-training and fine-tuning work, and Chinese labs are clearly going to use them more over time, partly by necessity. But for the biggest pretraining runs, I think the top Chinese labs would still rather have Nvidia hardware if they can get it, and the ones doing the most impressive work have mostly done it on Nvidia. The interesting thing to watch is how fast that gap closes. Necessity is a strong forcing function, and if a lab like DeepSeek really commits to building its stack around Ascend, I wouldn't bet against them making it work better than outsiders expect.

r001.rationale: It says Huawei Ascend chips are “genuinely usable” for inference and that serving a trained model on them is workable.

r002.rationale: It describes frontier training as difficult and mentions post-training and fine-tuning, but does not say training is currently limited to very small models.

r003.rationale: It discusses serving models on Ascend, but does not identify access to Huawei chips as a way for established service providers to serve more customers.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure, so I think the honest answer is that it's a mixed picture, and you have to separate inference from training because they're really different problems.

On inference, Huawei's Ascend chips are genuinely useful today. Inference is a more forgiving workload. You can tolerate lower per-chip efficiency if you can just throw more chips at it, and that's largely what the Chinese labs have done. DeepSeek, for example, has been serving models on Ascend hardware, and the open-source ecosystem around things like vLLM and MindSpore has gotten good enough that you can run a modern mixture-of-experts model and get reasonable throughput. It's not as efficient as an H100 or a B200 per watt or per dollar, but if your constraint is access rather than cost, it works. And the thing people underestimate is that for a lot of deployments in China, the real question isn't "is this as good as Nvidia," it's "can I get Nvidia at all." So the practical usefulness there is high.

Training is a much harder story. Frontier pretraining is extremely sensitive to the whole stack: the interconnect, the memory bandwidth, the software maturity, the ability to debug a loss spike at 3 a.m. across thousands of chips. Nvidia has a decade of CUDA, NCCL, and all the little tooling that makes a big run survivable. Huawei's software is improving fast, but when I talk to people who've actually tried to do large runs on Ascend, the common theme is that you lose a lot of time to engineering overhead. The chips themselves may have decent peak numbers, but the realized utilization is lower, and the clusters are harder to keep stable. That compounds at scale.

So where I land is that Huawei is not going to produce the best training chip in the world in the next year or two, but that may not matter as much as people think. The Chinese labs have shown they can be very creative with constrained compute. If they do the big pretraining run on whatever Nvidia hardware they have, and then do the post-training, the reinforcement learning, and all the serving on domestic chips, that's a pretty viable strategy. And the gap closes every year because the software side is the part that's most responsive to effort, and there's a lot of effort going into it.

The thing I'd watch is less the chip benchmarks and more whether a Chinese lab openly says "we trained this frontier model end to end on Ascend." When that happens and the model is competitive, that's the real signal. Until then I'd say: strong for inference, workable but painful for training, and improving faster than most people in the US assume.

r001.rationale: The response says Ascend chips are “genuinely useful today” for inference and describes serving modern models on them with reasonable throughput.

r002.rationale: It describes training as harder and more engineering-intensive, but does not say Huawei chips are currently limited to very small models.

r003.rationale: It says Huawei chips can support serving when Nvidia access is constrained, but does not state that this lets established providers serve more customers.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate inference from training. For inference, the question is whether you can run a particular model reliably at a competitive cost and latency. Huawei chips can be useful there, especially if you’re willing to optimize the software for the hardware. You don’t necessarily need the best chip in the world to serve a useful language model.

Training is harder, particularly at the frontier. You need thousands of chips communicating efficiently, and the whole system has to keep running reliably for a long time. So it’s not just about the performance of an individual chip; it’s the networking, memory, software stack, and how quickly engineers can diagnose failures.

My assessment would be that they’re a practical option for some inference workloads, while large-scale training is a much more demanding test. I’d want to see sustained utilization, reliability, and total cost on a real workload before making a stronger claim.

r001.rationale: The response says Huawei chips can be useful for inference and calls them a practical option for some inference workloads.

r002.rationale: It describes large-scale training as demanding but does not say training is currently limited to very small models.

r003.rationale: It does not identify access to Huawei chips as a way for established language-model service providers to serve more customers.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate inference from training, because they’re quite different problems. For inference, Huawei chips can be useful if you can get the model running efficiently on the hardware. You have a fixed model, you can optimize the deployment, and you can put a lot of engineering effort into a workload that you’re going to run repeatedly.

Training is a harder test. It’s not just whether one chip has competitive performance; it’s whether thousands of chips can communicate reliably, whether the software supports the operations you need, and how much time your researchers spend debugging the infrastructure. A chip can look good on paper and still be difficult to use for a large training run.

So I wouldn’t dismiss Huawei, particularly for serving models within China. But I’d want to see sustained performance on real workloads before concluding that the hardware is interchangeable with Nvidia. The practical question is: how much useful work can you get done, at what cost, and with how much engineering effort?
